common_name: Mendoza's Graptopetalum (Trailing Blush-Pink Bead Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Root stem or leaf cuttings in spring in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix; the stems naturally decumbent or pendent, so this species is best grown in a hanging basket or spilling over the edge of a raised container.

directions: Plant in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in full sun to bright light, watering thoroughly and then letting the mix dry out completely before the next watering. This Mexican species forms small, tight rosettes of pale grey-green leaves along wiry stems that trail, arch, or sprawl rather than staying upright, and the leaf color shifts to a soft blush pink under strong sun and cooler temperatures. Small white star-shaped flowers appear in loose branched clusters in summer. Because the stems lengthen and root wherever they touch soil, it makes an easy groundcover or basket subject that is simple to propagate from broken-off stem pieces.

planting.note: Separate rooted offsets in spring into gritty, mineral succulent mix; native to shaded cliffs and canyon walls in Arizona and northern Mexico, it tolerates cooler, drier conditions and part shade better than most graptopetalums in this collection.

directions: Grow in bright light to partial shade in gritty, well-drained mineral soil, allowing it to dry fully between waterings. Rosettes stay compact at only about 2 inches tall and 4 inches across, with thick, upward-curving leaves that shift from blue-gray in shade to dusty pink or yellow-pink under strong sun, and the plant offsets freely to form small colonies. In summer a branched flowering stalk rises to about a foot, carrying blooms in an unusual mix of red, pink, and white. Because it naturally grows tucked into rock crevices and on shaded cliff faces, it appreciates slightly more shelter from midday sun than typical desert succulents.
sources: Kew Science Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; older stems become lax and benefit from a raised pot or light staking as they lengthen.

directions: Plant in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light, soaking thoroughly and then letting the soil dry out completely before watering again. Unlike the powdery, glaucous moonstones already represented in this collection, this species carries slender, straight, cylindrical leaves up to 6 inches long that stay solid green with essentially no waxy bloom even in strong light, giving it a smoother, glossier look than its relatives. Leaves are borne in loose rosettes along stems that elongate and lean over with age, so older plants take on a shrubby, sprawling form. It hybridizes readily with the more common Pachyphytum oviferum, and cuttings root easily in the growing season.

planting.note: Root offsets or leaf cuttings in spring in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light; as a named hybrid cultivar it does not come true from seed, so propagation is strictly vegetative.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light, letting the soil dry out fully between waterings. Bred by California hobbyist Robert Grim from Graptopetalum amethystinum crossed with Echeveria colorata and first named in 1988, this hybrid forms compact, short-stemmed rosettes of pale blue-green leaves that develop pink blush along the tips and margins in strong light, an opalescent shift in color that gives the cultivar its name. It clumps by offsetting at the base rather than trailing, and in late spring sends up branched stalks of small yellow flowers tinged pink. Keep it in bright, unfiltered light for the best color contrast and bring containers indoors below about 20 degrees F.

planting.note: Root offsets or leaf cuttings in spring in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix; as a nursery-bred hybrid it must be propagated vegetatively rather than from seed.

directions: Grow in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light, allowing the mix to dry out completely between waterings. Raised from a cross between Graptopetalum paraguayense and Echeveria derenbergii, this older hybrid produces pale, chalky blue-white rosettes of thick, pointed leaves with a smooth, porcelain-like sheen, and is sold under the common name Porcelain Plant for that finish. Its stems sprawl and offset loosely rather than forming a single tight clump, giving mature plants a looser, spreading habit than the more upright 'Fred Ives' and 'Debbie' hybrids already in the collection. Handle it carefully, since the powdery leaf coating marks easily and dropped leaves readily root to form new plants.

common_name: Powder Puff Pachyveria (Chalky Blue-Lavender Chunky Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Root offsets or leaf cuttings in spring in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light; this hybrid cultivar is propagated only vegetatively.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light, watering deeply and then letting the soil dry out completely before watering again. Bred in the 1970s from Pachyphytum oviferum crossed with Echeveria cante, this hybrid carries thick, plump, egg-shaped leaves in a pale, chalky blue-lavender that is even chunkier than either moonstones or the Little Jewel hybrid already in the collection. It clumps low and slow, staying compact for years before needing division, and produces short stalks of yellow-and-pink bell flowers in spring. The heavy surface bloom rubs off with handling, so display it where it will not be brushed or knocked.
